3. The learned Munsif, on evidence adduced before him, found that the holding was an occupancy raiyati holding and accordingly he allowed both the cases for pre-emption. The learned District Judge, on appeal, set aside the judgment and order of the learned Munsifand dismissed those cases and disallowed pre-emption on a finding that the holding was a Korfa (under-raiyati) holding with occupancy right and that pre-emption under section 26F of the B. T. Act was not available. Thereafter the respondents, i.e., the pre-emptors, obtained two Rules. A learned Single Judge of the Dacca High Court made the Rules absolute on a finding that the Korfa (under-raiyati tenancy) under pre-emption was "upgraded to a raiyati tenancy since 14.4.56 as the rent-receiving interests of  the immediate landlord, who was a raiyat, stood acquired with effect from 14.4.56 under general Notification under section 3 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. He further found that section 26F of the B. T. Act was fully applicable to these cases as the sale took place on 4.12.1959 and, 5.12.1959 and the applications for pre-emption were filed on 3.12.1962 when B. T. Act was in force and was still governing the field. 

 4. Leave was granted to consider (1) whether prior to coming into operation of Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act (hereinafter referred to as the Act), the Korfa (under-raiyati) tenancy became upgraded to a raiyati tenancy on and from 14.4.56 simply because by the general Notification under section 3 of the Act the rent-receiving interests stood acquired with effect from 14.4.56 and (ii) whether, in case of upgrading of under-raiyati to a raiyati in the above circumstance, pre-emption under section 26F of the B. T. Act was available in the instant case. 

 5. Mr. Siddique Ahmed Chowdhury, learned Counsel for the appellants firstly contended that it was wrong to hold that the Korfa (under raiyati) tenancy was upgraded to a raiyati tenancy since 14. 4. 56 when by a general Notification under section 3 of the Act all rent-receiving interests were acquired by the Government. He urgued that even after acquisition of the rent-receiving interests of the raiyat under section 3 of the Act, the Korfa tenant, that is the under-raiyat who was a. tenant under the raiyat, continued to be so under the B. T. Act till Part V of the Act came into operation. The learned Counsel pointed out that in the District of Chittagong wherein lies the land in question, Part V of the Act came into operation on 1.8.63 and since that date B. T. Act stood repealed as provided in section 80 of the Act. So, it was contended that prior to 1.8.63, B. T. Act was in force in that area with all incidents of tenancies thereunder and that the under-raiyat retained the status of an under-raiyat within the meaning of section 4 of the B. T. Act till 1.8.63. The learned Counsel thereby tried to impress upon us that it is not correct to say that the rent-receiving interest of the raiyat having been acquired, the raiyat disappeared from the field and that the under-raiyat was upgraded to the status of a raiyat. In support of his contention reference was made to some provisions of the Act as well as to some Rules with particular reference to sub-section (J) of section 24 of the Act and rules 18 and 61 of the State Acquisition Rules, 1951 (herein-after called the Rules) to show that the original status of the different kinds of tenants remained unchanged till Part V of the Act came into operation. In order to appreciate the contention of the learned Counsel, sub-section (1) of section 24 of the Act. and rules 18 and 61 of the Rules are quoted below :- 

 "In preparing or revising a record-of-rights under this Chapter, the Revenue-officer shall, subject to the provisions of sub-sections (2), (3) and (4), presume the rent, payable in respect of any land held by a raiyat or an under-raiyat in the area to which such record relates at the time of preparation or revision of such record, to be fair and equitable." 

 (b) the classes to which each such tenant or occupant belongs that is to say, whether he i.s a proprietor, tenure-holder raiyat holding at fixed rates, settled raiyat, occupancy raiyat, non-occupancy raiyat, under-raiyat with or without a right of occupancy, or a non-agricultural tenant, and if he is a tenure holder, whether he is a permanent tenure-holder or not, and whether his rent is liable to enhancement during the continuance of his tenure .... ., 

 "After the final publication of the compensation-assessment-roll, the Collector shall assign a touzi number to all the lands under one Tahsil and inform the Revenue Officer accordingly. The Revenue Officer shall, thereafter, re-arrange the khatians under that touzi number by eliminating therefrom the entire chain of interests of rent-receivers and showing therein only the tenants who will come directly under the provincial Government." 

 6. It appears that mention of the different classes of tenants or occupants has been made in the above quoted provisions of law. It was argued that sub-section (1) of section 24 of the Act clearly indicates that on under-raiyati holding would remain in existence at the time of the preparation of the record-of-rights which would be subsequent to the Notification under section 3 of the Act. Rule 18 provides for the preparation or revision of the record-of-rights on the basis of which the compensation Assessment-roll would be prepared and published and rule 61 says that the different classes of tenancies would not cease to exist with publication of the Notification under section 3 of the Act and that entire chain of interests of rent-receivers would be eliminated only after the publication of the Compensation Assessment-roll. Thereafter a Notification would be published under sub-section (2) of section 43 declaring that the compensation assessment-roll in respect of that area had been finally published and after this publication of Notification, the whole of Part V of the Act would come into operation. The sum and substance of the contention of the learned Counsel is that raiyaji interest did not cease to exist and that under-raiyat was not upgraded before Part V came into operation. With a view to strengthen his argument the learned Counsel relied on a decision in Afran Ali Sheikh's case reported in 14 D.L.R. (Dacca)791. It is a Single Bench decision by Idris, J. of the Dacca High Court. The said case was under section 26P of the B. T. Act. In that case the question arose as to whether there was an automatic elevation of under-raiyats to the status of raiyats with effect from 14.4.56 when all rent-receiving interests vested in the Government. The learned Judge held that publication of Notification under section 3 of the Act did not eliminate the different classes of tenancies till publication of the compensation assessment-roll, i.e., till Part V of the Act came into operation. In coming to that decision Idris, J. it appears, relied on an unreported decision by Asir, J., in Civil Revision Case Nos.1129 and 1130 of 1960 of the Dacca High Court. On the authority of the decision of Idris, J. and the provisions of law referred to above, the learned Counsel submitted that pre-emption was not available in the present case to an under-raiyati even if he had occupancy right. 

 7. On the other hand, Mr. M. A. Rouf, appearing for the respondents argued that in deciding this point, the general scheme of the Act is to be taken into consideration. The general scheme of the Act is that for the purpose of taking over all interests that are liable to be acquired under the Act, preparation of record-of-rights is to be made and after final publication of the record-of-rights, assessment of compensation of the acquirable interests is to be made and finally published. It, however, seems that an exception has been made with regard to rent-receiving interests and special provisions for acquisition of the interests of certain rent-receivers have been made in Chapter II of Part II of the Act. According to the provisions of this Chapter, rent-receiving interests can be acquired by publication of Notification under section 3 of the Act even before the general provisions of the Act are given effect to, that is, before preparation of the record-of-rights and preparation and publication of the Compensation Assessment-roll. It may also be pointed out that according to the provisions of section 3 of the Act, before introduction of the sub-section (2a) in section 3 by way of amendment, Notification under section 3 was to be published with reference to particular estates, taluks, tenures, holdings and tenancies and in respect of all rent-receivers whose properties were under the management of Court of Wards Act, 1879. Sub-section (2a) was enacted and introduced in section 3 of the Act by Ordinance No. III of 1956. This provision, namely, sub-section (2a) empowers the Government to publish Notification under section 3 in respect of rent-receivers by name or by reference to areas wherein they have interests or in such other manner as the Government might determine. It is after this amendment that general Notification dated 2nd April, 1956 were issued District-wise in regard to all rent-receiving interests which thereafter vested in the Government with effect from 14.4.56 in terms of those Notifications. So, Mr. Rouf submitted that it was futile to argue that these interests, which were the subject-matter of the general Notifications, contained even after 14th April, 1956 and that they did not vest in the Government. His contention was that in the instant case the rent-receiving interests of the raiyat legally vested in the Government which became the proprietor by virtue of acquisition of the said interests. Accordingly, from 14. 4. 56 the Government alone became entitled, under the law, to receive the rent. The previous rent-receivers became divested of the right to receive rent and consequently they disappeared from the scene. On this point reference was made to sub-section (4)(e) of section 3 which runs thus :— 

 "all tenants holding lands in such estates, taluks, tenures, holdings or tenancies directly under the rent-receiver specified in the notification under sub-section (1), shall become tenants directly under the Provincial Government and shall pay rent at the existing rate, in respect of the rent-paying lands so held by them to the Provincial Government and not to any body else." 

 8. In support of the argument advanced by Mr. Rouf reliance was placed on a decision of a Division Bench of the Dacca High Court in the case of Mubashor Ali in 19 D.L.R. (Dacca) 271 in which it was held that after the general Notification under section 3 of the Act which came into operation on 14. 4. 56 all rent-receiving interests stood acquired by the Government and that there was automatic elevation of under-raiyats to the status of raiyats. It was pointed out by Mr. Rouf that the decision of Idris, J., and that by Asir, J., were noticed by the Division Bench in Mubasher Ali's case. It is to be noted that similar contentions, as have been pressed in the instant case by the learned Counsel for the appellants, were urged in Mubasher Ali's case too. The Division Bench, it appears, considered the provisions of the Act which were considered by Idris, J. The said Bench also considered the provisions of sub-section(2) of Section 43 and those of sections 79 and 80 of the Act and observed as follows :— 

 10. Mr. Rouf submitted that from the decision made in Mubasher Alis case it is clear that the Division Bench did not agree with the view expressed by Idris, J. in Arfan Ali Sheikh's case. In view of the said decision, Mr. Rouf tried to impress upon us that the effect of acquisition of rent-receiving interests under section 3 of the Act was the total elimination of all rent-receivers and that those who had no rent-receiving interests, remained on the land as tenants under the Government. In the instant case the immediate rent-receiver was the raiyat who, on account of acquisition of his rent-receiving interests, disappeared from the class of tenants and the under-raiyat under him became the raiyat under the Government and became legally entitled to claim pre-emption, if not otherwise barred. 

 11. Learned Counsel for the appellants, however, contended that there being conflicting decisions of the High Court on the above question, it is desirable that this Court should finally settle the conflict. According to him, till Part V of the Act comes into operation, the different classes of tenants under section 4 of the B. T. Act would continue in spite of acquisition of the rent-receiving interests by Notification under section 3 of the Act. In support of his contention, reference was made to sub-section(1) of section 81 of the Act. Sub-section (1) of section 81 of the Act occurs in Part V thereof and reads as follows :— 

 "(1) On and from the first day of the agricultural year immediately following the publication of a notification in the official Gazette under sub-section (2) of section 43 declaring that a Compensation Assessment-roll has been finally published, there shall, within the area to which such roll relates, be only one class of tenants of agricultural land, namely, raiyats, and the rights and liabilities of every such raiyat shall be regulated by the provisions of this Part." 

 12. It is evident that the word "raiyats" in the original sub-section (1) was later substituted by the word "maliks". Whatever may be nomenclature of the holder of the land under the Government, there is no dispute that the only authority which is entitled to get rent is the Government. Virtually the holder of the land paying rent to the Government is a tenant according to the definition under section 2(27) of the Act. The provision of the present sub-section (1) of section 81 merely indicates that after acquisition of rent-receiving interests those who would remain on the land would pay rent for the land to the Government and would hold the land under the Government as maliks and the different classes of tenants under section 4 of the B. T. Act would go and the B. T. Act would be repealed as a whole. Accordingly, the raiyati interest which was a rent-receiving interest in the instant case, vested in the Government by virtue of the acquisition of the said interest and the under-raiyat, in view of the sub-section (4)(e) of section 3 of the Act, became a tenant directly under the Government. This tenant under the original sub-section (1) of section 81 was designated as raiyat and under the present sub-section (1) of section 81 as "malik." 

 13. The next contention urged by the learned Counsel for the appellants was that in the absence of any specific provision in the Act conferring the right of pre-emption to an upgraded under-raiyat as a raiyat, no right of preemption under section 26F of the B.T. Act can be available to such a raiyat under the said Act and that in claiming pre-emption in the instant case the respondents sought to take advantage of two laws, i.e., section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and section 26F of the B. T. Act. It was pointed out that the respondents firstly claimed that under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act the status of the under-raiyat was raised to that of a raiyat after acquisition of the rent-receiving interests of the latter and accordingly secondly, they sought to obtain pre-emption of the raiyati interest under section 26F of the B. T. Act. It was, therefore, submitted that the respondents should not be allowed to take advantage of both the laws according to convenience only to suit their purpose, r.e., the upgrading of the under-raiyat to the status of a raiyat under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and the relief by way of pre-emption under the B. T. Act. lie accordingly urged for dismissal of the applications for pre-emption of the disputed land. This contention of the learned Counsel does not appear to be tenable inasmuch as the right which  became available to the respondents was not their own creation. The said right was created by a statute. It is all undenying fact that the raiyati interests in the present case in view of the under raiyat there under was a rent-receiving interest within the meaning of the Act. The rent-receiving interests of the raiyat, as already stated; vested in the Government. The Government became the proprietor by virtue of acquisition of the said interests. Thereafter the rent-receiving raiyat was divested of his right and consequently disappeared from the field. Naturally the under-raiyat was automatically upgraded as a raiyat under the Government, there being no intermediate interest in between. Part V of the Act not having come into operation at the time the transfers in the instant case were made and the applications for pre-emption having been filed when the B.T. Act was in force, the right to claim pre-emption could be exercised under the law in force.
